o1.said: How three p p lights a frame: rasterized visibility, ray-traced light, and three ways to reuse a ray.

p1.said: A path tracer lights a pixel by following light backwards, bounce after bounce, until it hits a lamp. Most random paths never get there.

p2.said: So a clean image needs thousands of paths per pixel. three p p's Vulkan renderer spends a few, and reuses them. Here is how.

g1.said: What the camera sees is not traced at all. It is rasterized into a G buffer: every pixel's normal, colour, depth and object.

d1.said: Light straight from the lamp is summed exactly. Only the shadows need rays: a ray or two per pixel, aimed at random points on the lamp.

b1.said: Bounce light and reflections add a few more. One frame of all of it, with no reuse, boils like this.

t1.said: Reuse one: time. Each pixel averages its past frames, found through the motion vectors, so the image settles even while the camera moves.

t2.said: Where the ball uncovers the floor, there is no past to use, and the grain comes back behind it.

s1.said: Reuse two: neighbours. Each pixel is blended with nearby pixels on the same surface, reaching further with every pass.

c1.said: Reuse three: a cache. Thousands of probes hold the light that bounces around the room, and a slice of them is updated every frame.

c2.said: Change the lamp, and the bounce light follows in under a second.

r1.said: Shiny surfaces add one ray around the mirror direction, blurred more the rougher they are.

k1.said: All of it runs in real time on a laptop GPU. A few rays per pixel, and the rest borrowed: from the past, the neighbours and a cache.
